newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU expected to say no to Kesko/Tuko deal.
newsitem.headline: EU expected to say no to Kesko/Tuko deal.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to rule next Wednesday against the merger between Finnish wholesaler and retailer Kesko and its rival Tuko, European Union sources said on Friday.
"There will be a negative decision," one source predicted.
The EU executive was expected to say at next week's regular meeting that the merger in its present form would not be compatible with the bloc's competition rules, the sources said.
In Helsinki, Kesko spokesman Erkki Heikkinen said, "We have no comment, no comment at all."

Kesko and Tuko are Finnish wholesalers and retailers of daily consumer goods, including foodstuffs, clothes, and hardware. At 1133 GMT, the Kesko share traded 1.5 markka ($0.33) lower at 65 markka after earlier reaching a day high of 67.1 markka.
In late October, Kesko proposed selling its Tukospar unit in response to the Commission's preliminary ruling in mid-September that the merger could be against EU rules.
The unit to be formed and sold would have net sales from wholesale operations worth 4.5 billion markka ($993.4 million) which is equal to about 40 percent of Tuko's 1995 net sales.

But EU sources said earlier this month this would not be enough for the Commission to approve the deal and Kesko would have to come up with a new proposal. One source did not rule out Kesko's proposing more radical remedies to win EU approval.

The Commission made it clear it was worried about the merger when it launched an in-depth investigation in July, following the initial one-month routine review, and has since expressed fears the deal would lead to a dominant market position.
On Thursday, EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert declined to comment on the case, saying only that he believed the decision would be taken on Wednesday.
The Commission vets corporate deals to see whether they could harm competition in the 15-nation EU and has blocked five deals since the EU merger regulation came into force in 1990.
Investigation of the Kesko deal, which was announced in May, was handed over by the Finnish Office of Free Competition as Finland does not have its own merger regulation.

The deal would make Kesko, which reported 1995 annual group sales of 26.5 billion markka ($5.85 billion), into Finland's third largest company in terms of net sales. Kesko said the deal would push it into 20th position among European retailers from 41st position in 1993.
Tuko's annual group sales are around 11.4 billion markka (1$=4.5335 markka)
